- **ap**: As AIPAC's brand became politically toxic and public opinion toward Israel cratered among key American demographics, the Israeli government made a structural decision: build a direct influence operation in the United States, registered under FARA, at a scale that dwarfs AIPAC's own spending in specific domains. Israel has spent more than $100 million on foreign lobbying efforts under FARA in the U.S. since 2023, hiring 17 new firms in 2024 and 2025 alone. The largest single contract — $46.5 million — went to Clock Tower X, the firm of former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale. The operation's primary target audience is not American voters. It is artificial intelligence training data. This is the most consequential blind spot in the simulation: a parallel, registered, legal influence operation targeting the information infrastructure itself.
- **ap**: … Clock Tower X LLC is a boutique digital influence company owned by Brad Parscale — Donald Trump's digital director in 2016 and campaign manager for his 2020 presidential run. In September 2025, the global advertising agency Havas — acting on behalf of Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs — hired Clock Tower X at an initial rate of $1.5 million per month.
- **ap**: The honest complication, and it is substantial. Trump campaigned actively against Massie over their long-running feud, calling him the worst congressman in the country in a barrage of posts before the primary. Trump advisers LaCivita and Fabrizio raised over $2 million for a MAGA KY PAC, and a Trump-adviser-created PAC spent more than $7 million on attack ads [cite:lpm_massie][cite:cd_massie_fara]. Total spending reached about $37 million, the most expensive House primary in American history. Attributing the defeat solely to AIPAC would be an overclaim the evidence does not support — as The Intercept put it, the money may have mattered less to Republican primary voters than Trump's hostility [cite:intercept_massie].
- **ap**: After the result, AIPAC posted publicly: "Massie has been one of the most consistently hostile voices in Congress toward the U.S.-Israel relationship and the millions of Americans who support it. Our community was proud to support Gallrein and help ensure Massie's defeat" [cite:intercept_massie]. This is the single most evidentially valuable sentence in the module. Where the causal question is otherwise contested by the Trump confounder, the organization itself asserts a causal role in the outcome — in its own voice, in public, as an achievement. That is an organizational statement, not an inference drawn by critics.

The mechanism this tier illustrates is uncomfortable for anyone writing critically about the subject, this module included: critical coverage transmits the vocabulary too. A reader who learns the word Cathedral from a hostile profile has still learned the word, and the framework's terms spread through the act of debunking them.
- **p25**: During the 2024 campaign Trump distanced himself from Project 2025 energetically and repeatedly, and his campaign leadership issued statements warning against anyone claiming to represent his agenda through it [cite:npr]. Many voters took that at face value — reasonably, since it was stated directly. The scenes that follow set that against the documented record of what happened after January 2025, keeping the two visibly separate rather than resolving one into the other.
- **p25**: The disavowal was real, public and repeated. Trump made an energetic effort on the campaign trail to distance himself from Project 2025 [cite:washweek], and campaign leadership Susie Wiles and Chris LaCivita issued a statement that reports of the project's demise would be welcomed and that anyone misrepresenting their influence with Trump would not fare well [cite:npr]. This module does not treat the disavowal as insincere — that would be an intent claim about a named person, which carries the tightest evidentiary ceiling in the protocol. It reports that it was said.
- **p25**: In July 2024 Heritage announced that Paul Dans, Project 2025's director, was stepping down after Trump became angered by reporting tying him to the plan, and that the project's policy operations were concluding [cite:npr]. Heritage president Kevin Roberts stated the policy work had always been set to conclude after the party conventions. Read alone, this looks like the project ending, and it was widely reported that way at the time.
- **p25**: Two overstatements circulate in critical coverage and this module rejects both. That every Trump-administration action implements Project 2025 — many actions have independent origins, and the plan's own authors did not invent conservative immigration or deregulatory policy. And that a single headline percentage is authoritative — the trackers use different denominators and thresholds, and a fact-check found that variation drives most of the apparent disagreement [cite:factually25]. Adopting either overstatement would make the documented findings easier to dismiss.
- **p25**: Heritage announced in July 2024 that Paul Dans was stepping down after Trump became angered by reporting tying him to the plan, and that Project 2025's policy operations were concluding. Heritage president Kevin Roberts said the policy work had always been set to conclude after the party conventions[cite:npr]. The Trump campaign's response, from Susie Wiles and Chris LaCivita, was that reports of the project's demise would be welcomed and should serve as notice to anyone misrepresenting their influence[cite:npr].
- **ep**: Giuffre was recruited around 2000 while working as a spa attendant at Mar-a-Lago, aged sixteen. She became the case's most prominent public accuser, and her sworn allegations in civil litigation produced much of the documentary record this module rests on. She stated that Trump, whose property it was, did not participate in any misconduct and was friendly to her — reported here because the module applies its standard in both directions.
- **ep**: Landon Thomas Jr.'s New York magazine profile, titled around the idea of an international moneyman of mystery, is the key contemporaneous document of this period. It contains Trump's quote describing him as a terrific guy who liked beautiful women as much as he did, many on the younger side. The profile is notable for what it establishes: his opacity was already the publicly known feature of him in 2002, and was treated as intriguing rather than alarming.
- **ep**: Acosta became Secretary of Labor in the Trump administration. He defended the agreement as appropriate given what prosecutors knew and could prove at the time, particularly the reluctance of many victims to testify — his position, stated publicly and on the record, and reported here as such. He faced sustained questioning before a House appropriations panel in April 2019 and resigned in July 2019, days after Epstein's federal arrest in New York. Whether the agreement was defensible on its merits is genuinely contested; that the victims were not told about it is not contested, because a court ruled on it.
- **ep**: Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche — previously Donald Trump's personal criminal defence attorney — personally interviewed Maxwell over two days at the US Attorney's office in Tallahassee in late July 2025. DOJ granted her limited immunity to discuss her case and released a transcript. Senators Whitehouse and Durbin wrote that it is highly unusual, if not unprecedented, for the second-ranking official at the Justice Department to conduct such an interview rather than a line prosecutor familiar with the case. The interview followed the July memo in which DOJ and the FBI announced no further Epstein documents would be released.
- **ep**: Trump and Epstein were socially associated across roughly fifteen years, documented in photographs, event footage, and contemporaneous quotes. In a 2002 New York magazine profile Trump described Epstein as a terrific guy who was a lot of fun to be with, and said he liked beautiful women as much as Trump did, many of them on the younger side. That quote is genuine and frequently cited. It establishes a friendship and a documented characterization; it is Tier 3 in this module's scheme — association, not conduct.
- **ep**: The relationship broke down in the early-to-mid 2000s, with reporting tying it to competition over a Palm Beach property that Trump outbid Epstein for. Trump has said he barred Epstein from Mar-a-Lago. The rupture is documented and predates Epstein's 2006 arrest, which matters for reading the association: it ended before the criminal exposure became public, rather than after.
- **ep**: The most important fact in this scene and the one most often omitted from both sides of the argument. Giuffre was recruited at Mar-a-Lago, where she worked as a spa attendant — so Trump's property is where the recruitment occurred. And Giuffre, the case's most prominent accuser, stated that Trump did not participate in any misconduct and was friendly to her. She was the person best placed to accuse him and she declined to. Under this module's tiering that is dispositive: no sworn allegation exists against him, so no allegation is carried.
- **ep**: Trump's name appears in released materials, as do hundreds of others across manifests, correspondence and contact records. The 2025 releases also produced a contested birthday-album item attributed to him, which he has disputed. Per the standard set two scenes earlier, appearance in the files establishes association and nothing more — and the module applies that identically to him and to everyone else in those documents. Applying it selectively in either direction would invalidate it everywhere.
- **ep**: The live structural finding, and it is about office rather than association. Trump signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act into law on November 19, 2025 after it passed 427–1 and by unanimous consent. His Justice Department then missed the statutory deadline, and by mid-2026 the Act's own Republican co-author, Rep. Thomas Massie, was stating that the Department continues to unlawfully withhold over three million files. A president signed a disclosure mandate; the executive branch he heads is accused by the bill's Republican author of defying it. That is documented, current, and independent of anything about the 1990s.
- **ep**: Bondi appeared before the House Judiciary Committee for more than five hours over the Department's handling of the files. Survivors sat behind her in the room. She did not offer them an apology. She traded personal attacks with committee members, calling Rep. Jamie Raskin a washed-up loser lawyer and accusing Rep. Thomas Massie — the Republican co-author of the Transparency Act — of Trump derangement syndrome. This is the hearing you watched, and the account of it is not a characterisation by critics: the exchanges are on the record and were reported identically across outlets.
- **ep**: In March 2026 the House Oversight Committee subpoenaed Bondi over the Department's handling of the files, with five Republicans joining Democrats in the vote. In April 2026 Trump fired her. On May 29, 2026 she gave a closed-door transcribed interview to House Oversight, telling the panel that redaction errors were made, that she had been assured by the reviewing team that only non-responsive, privileged or duplicative material was withheld, and that to the best of her knowledge the Department produced everything required. She refused to discuss the President's involvement in the handling of the files. Todd Blanche, her deputy, became acting Attorney General.
- **ep**: FBI staff were reportedly instructed to flag mentions of Trump while reviewing the document trove, and the Wall Street Journal reported that Bondi told Trump in May 2025 that his name appeared in the files. Two months later came the memo announcing no further disclosure. This module reports these as named-outlet reporting rather than as established fact — DOJ has not confirmed the flagging instruction — and reports the sequence without asserting causation between the briefing and the memo, because no document establishes that link.
- **ep**: In November 2025, despite the July memo stating no further investigation was warranted, Trump ordered Bondi to investigate Epstein's ties to Bill Clinton and other prominent Democrats. She said the Department would pursue it with urgency and integrity and assigned it to the US Attorney in Manhattan. The sequence is documented: the Department found no basis to investigate uncharged third parties in July, and in November was directed to investigate a specific set of named third parties. Both cannot rest on the same evidentiary standard.
- **fed2**: The decision's significance is sharpened by what the Court did on the same day. In Trump v. Slaughter it held the President may remove members of traditionally independent agencies such as the FTC — and simultaneously carved the Federal Reserve out as an exception to that new rule, describing it as uniquely structured. Governors may not be removed for policy disagreement or at will. The Fed's independence now rests on an explicit constitutional carve-out rather than on convention.
- **fed2**: Four justices would have permitted the removal, and the ruling did not preclude a further attempt if the President supplies evidence and an opportunity to respond. The case returns to the lower courts. Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee, warned during argument that accepting the government's position — that the President alone defines cause, with no judicial review and no process — would weaken if not shatter the Fed's independence. Powell called it perhaps the most important legal case in the Fed's 113-year history.
- **fed2**: Documented: a twelve-vote FOMC with a permanent seven-member public majority; rate control now administered through interest on reserve balances and an overnight reverse repo floor rather than through reserve scarcity; a multi-trillion balance sheet operating as a second instrument; commercial banks creating the large majority of money by lending, with the Fed pricing rather than issuing; a statutory dual mandate pursued with one lever; transcripts released on a five-year lag; and Trump v. Cook decided 5–4 on June 29, 2026, carving the Fed out of a same-day ruling permitting removal at other independent agencies.
- **fed2**: Named gaps: FOMC deliberation is statutorily exempt from GAO review and transcripts arrive five years late, so the reasoning behind current decisions is not externally verifiable in real time. The Powell Inspector General review was ongoing at build date. Trump v. Cook was remanded and a further removal attempt remains legally open. And the counterfactual problem is structural — there is no test of what a different decision would have produced.
- **fed2**: ⭐ 5 · Supreme Court — Trump v. Cook / Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026)
- **hillary**: Clinton serves on four major Senate committees — Armed Services, Budget, Environment and Public Works, and Health/Education/Labor/Pensions — and chairs the Democratic Steering and Outreach Committee (2003–2007). Her 2002 Iraq War authorization vote (era #11) remains the defining liability that will resurface in 2008. She addresses AIPAC's annual conference as a sitting Senator. On January 22, 2005, she and Bill Clinton attend Donald Trump's wedding to Melania Knauss at Mar-a-Lago — documented, extensively photographed, and a friendly relationship that will invert completely within a decade.
- **hillary**: The Iraq vote is sometimes remembered in hindsight as an outlier; the record shows it was part of a broad, bipartisan 2002 authorization vote. Separately, the Trump-Clinton relationship is now remembered as pure enmity — the photographic record from this exact period says otherwise.
- **hillary**: … 2002 Iraq War authorization vote; her committee assignments; her vote for the 2001 No Child Left Behind Act (87-10); her 2003 memoir *Living History* (~$8M advance). DOCUMENTED, extensively: she had a front-row seat at Trump's Jan. 22, 2005 wedding ceremony; Bill Clinton joined the Mar-a-Lago reception; multiple verified, widely-circulated photos show the two couples together smiling, including one with Bill's hand on Trump's shoulder and one with Trump's arm around Hillary. A fellow guest told NPR he watched her kiss the newlyweds and described her as 'very pleasant' with Trump. This module's full Senate voting record beyond these highlights remains a flagged, partially-built gap — the four committees and the Iraq/NCLB votes are now documented; a complete bill-by-bill pass has not been run.
- **hillary**: Both Clintons attended his Jan. 22, 2005 wedding to Melania Knauss; he had personally donated more than $4,000 to her Senate campaigns and at least $100,000 to the Clinton Foundation over the years. He kept a photo from the wedding on display in his own living room for years afterward, per a Harper's Bazaar profile of Melania Trump cited by TIME. This friendship inverts completely by the 2016 campaign (see era #14). [cite:politifact_trump_wedding][cite:time_trump_photo_display][cite:yahoo_photographic_proof]
- **hillary**: The Benghazi Committee's document requests surface Clinton's private email server; the FBI investigates 2015–16. July 5, 2016: FBI Director Comey calls her 'extremely careless' but recommends no charges; DOJ closes the matter July 6. August 2015: the DNC, Hillary Victory Fund, and her campaign sign a Joint Fundraising Agreement. October 2016: leaked Podesta emails show Donna Brazile forwarding debate questions to the campaign. Across the same campaign, the decade-old Trump friendship (era #12) completely and visibly reverses — the 2005 wedding photos become a talking point used against Trump by his own primary rivals, and his attacks on Clinton turn personal. November 8, 2016: she wins the popular vote by ~2.9 million but loses the Electoral College by ~77,000 combined votes in three states.
- **hillary**: This whole cluster gets flattened in multiple directions — either 'she got away with a crime,' 'this was all nothing,' or 'Trump and the Clintons were always enemies.' None of the three survive contact with the documented record.
- **hillary**: … 2015 agreement's actual terms and Brazile's own confirmed admission. DOCUMENTED (Trump): during the first GOP primary debate (Aug. 2015), Trump said the Clintons 'had no choice' but to attend his wedding given his donations to their causes, and separately told the *Daily Mail* he never received favors for the donations 'but they do kiss my ass' to get them — his own explanation, on the record. Biographers quoted by NPR describe his friendships generally as 'transactional.' Whether 'transactional' fully explains the documented warmth in the wedding photos (kissing, arms around each other, years of display in his own home) is CONTESTED interpretation, not settled fact — the photographic record is more effusive than a purely transactional donor relationship typically produces, and this module notes that tension without resolving it.
- **hillary**: Clinton's 2017 memoir *What Happened* and the launch of Onward Together (also 2017) set the frame for this era. She remains a public voice via opinion writing (a 2019 *Washington Post* op-ed on the Mueller Report; a Nov./Dec. 2020 *Foreign Affairs* piece, 'A National Security Reckoning'; a Jan. 2021 *Washington Post* op-ed, days after the Jan. 6 Capitol riot, arguing for Trump's impeachment), co-authors *The Book of Gutsy Women* with Chelsea Clinton (2019), and receives an honorary degree from Columbia University in 2022.
- **hillary**: Two things are true at once: Trump and the Clintons had a genuine, photographed friendship for over a decade, and separately, both Trump and Bill Clinton had their own independent, photographed social relationships with Jeffrey Epstein. The record supports neither collapsing these into one 'secret alliance' story nor pretending the friendship didn't happen.
- **hillary**: Donations $4,000+ to Senate campaigns; $100,000+ to the Foundation → Jan. 22, 2005 Trump-Knauss wedding, Palm Beach → Years of display Trump kept a wedding photo with the Clintons on display at home Hillary Clinton had a front-row seat at the ceremony; Bill Clinton joined the Mar-a-Lago reception. Multiple verified, widely-circulated photos show the two couples together — smiling, arms around each other. A fellow guest, Bo Dietl, told NPR he watched Hillary Clinton go over and kiss the newlyweds, describing her as 'very pleasant.'
- **hillary**: Trump's own on-record explanation: during the Aug. 2015 GOP primary debate he said the Clintons 'had no choice' given his donations; separately he told the Daily Mail he never got favors for the money 'but they do kiss my ass' to get it. Biographers Gwenda Blair and Michael D'Antonio, quoted by NPR, describe his friendships generally as transactional — he 'surrounds himself with people he perceives as winners.' That explanation is documented, but it sits in real tension with the photographic record: kissing, arms around each other, and a photo displayed in his own home for years is more effusive than a purely transactional donor relationship typically produces. This module states that tension rather than resolving it for the reader.
- **hillary**: This friendship is a separate documented thread from either man's Epstein exposure. No documented photo has surfaced showing Trump, Epstein, and (Bill) Clinton together in the same frame — what exists are three overlapping pairwise relationships (Trump-Epstein, Clinton-Epstein, Trump-Clinton), not one three-way connection. A December 2025 document release from Epstein's own estate did include images of both Trump and Bill Clinton (separately) alongside Epstein and Maxwell, among many other names (Bill Gates, Woody Allen, Steve Bannon) — none of the released photos depict wrongdoing, per the reporting on that release itself. Hillary Clinton does not appear in this Epstein-photo thread at all; her own, separate Epstein-related record is covered in era #16.
- **hillary**: Discipline — What the Record Shows and Does Not Shows: a real, extensively documented, decade-plus friendship between Trump and both Clintons, and its complete, documented reversal by 2016. Does not show: any documented three-way Trump-Epstein-Clinton connection, and does not show that the friendship's warmth is fully explained by transactional donor logic — that's an open, labeled tension, not a resolved finding.
- **fourthturn**: Steve Bannon made an entire documentary in 2010 based on this theory, years before he became one of Trump's top White House advisors [cite:wiki_howe]. The New York Times [cite:nyt_bannon] and Forbes [cite:forbes_bannon] both wrote about how much this specific book shaped how he saw politics. Of everyone in this scene, his connection is the most solid and well-documented.
- **fourthturn**: In 2010 — years before he worked in the White House — Bannon made a documentary film using this exact theory to explain the 2008 financial crash [cite:wiki_howe]. Later, once he was a top Trump advisor, the New York Times wrote a whole story connecting his worldview back to this specific book [cite:nyt_bannon], and Forbes wrote something similar [cite:forbes_bannon].

It survived an attempt to end it during Trump's first term through a lawsuit, got extended under Biden, and its current extension is set to run out on September 9, 2026 — literally tomorrow as we're building this [cite:uscis_tps_elsalvador][cite:fwd_tps][cite:documentedny_tps]. A Supreme Court ruling on June 25, 2026 cleared the way for the administration to end other countries' TPS, so El Salvador's actual status right now is genuinely uncertain — check uscis.gov directly before relying on this.

- **trumpbio**: Donald John Trump was born June 14, 1946, in Queens, New York, the fourth of five children of Fred and Mary Anne Trump. The family's wealth and real estate business — built by grandfather Frederick Trump and expanded by Fred Trump — is documented in full in the companion Ivanka Trump Architecture module, including the Pulitzer Prize-winning NYT investigation into the wealth-transfer mechanisms.
- **trumpbio**: Fourth of five children of Fred and Mary Anne Trump. This module traces his life strictly chronologically in five-year blocks, cross-referencing the companion family and business modules wherever content is already fully documented there rather than duplicating it.
- **trumpbio**: Fred Trump's real estate empire and the Pulitzer-winning NYT investigation into how wealth was transferred to his children are documented in full in the companion module.
- **trumpbio**: Trump grew up in Jamaica Estates, Queens. At 13, reportedly after disciplinary issues, his parents sent him to the New York Military Academy, a private boarding school, where he remained through high school.
- **trumpbio**: A private military boarding school in Cornwall-on-Hudson, NY. Trump has described the discipline of this period as formative; independent biographical detail on this specific period is comparatively thin relative to his adult record.
- **trumpbio**: Trump attended Fordham University for two years before transferring to the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, graduating in 1968. He registered for the draft in 1964 and received four student deferments through his college years, then a fifth medical deferment in 1968 for bone spurs in both heels — the diagnosis coming from a podiatrist who rented office space from Fred Trump.
- **trumpbio**: Selective Service records obtained by The Smoking Gun via FOIA in 2011 confirm the deferment sequence precisely. A later NYT investigation found the podiatrist's own daughters stated their father provided the bone-spur diagnosis as a "favor" to Fred Trump — and Trump's own former lawyer, Michael Cohen, has recounted Trump saying "You think I'm stupid? I wasn't going to Vietnam." Both the documented deferment sequence and this specific characterization of its origin are worth holding separately: the deferments themselves are confirmed by primary Selective Service records; the "favor" framing rests on a secondhand family account decades later.
- **trumpbio**: Transferred from Fordham after two years. Trump has at times described graduating "first in his class," a specific claim not supported by Penn's own records — Wharton did not rank undergraduates in this way at the time.
- **trumpbio**: A New York Times investigation found the daughters of Dr. Larry Braunstein — who rented office space from Fred Trump — stated their father provided the bone-spur diagnosis as a favor. [cite:pressreader_bonespurs] Michael Cohen has separately recounted Trump privately acknowledging the deferment was a deliberate way to avoid service. Both accounts are secondhand and postdate the events by decades — kept as documented claims, not elevated to the same evidentiary tier as the primary Selective Service records themselves.
- **trumpbio**: After graduating, Trump joined his father's company, Trump Management, becoming president in 1971. In 1973, while he held that role, the Nixon DOJ sued the company for racial discrimination against Black rental applicants — the earliest major legal case in his business record.
- **trumpbio**: Full documentation of the case — the specific allegations, the 1975 consent decree, and the 1978 follow-up suit — lives in the companion Trump Organization Architecture module's Scene t02, since Trump himself was a named respondent alongside the company.
- **trumpbio**: Trump's first major Manhattan project — a renovation of the derelict Commodore Hotel into the Grand Hyatt, aided by a then-unprecedented property tax abatement from the city — established him in Manhattan real estate. He married Czech model Ivana Zelníčková in 1977.
- **trumpbio**: Trump Tower opened on Fifth Avenue in 1983 — a luxury mixed-use tower that put Trump's own name on the building itself, establishing the personal-branding strategy that would define his business model for the rest of his career: licensing his name as much as building anything himself.
- **trumpbio**: A genuine commercial and architectural success. Marks the strategic shift toward licensing the Trump name itself as a product — the same underlying model later applied to the Gulf real estate deals documented in the companion Trump Organization module.
- **trumpbio**: The Art of the Deal (1987) made Trump a household name beyond real estate circles. In 1989, following the brutal rape and beating of a jogger in Central Park, Trump spent $85,000 on full-page newspaper ads in four NYC papers calling for the death penalty's reinstatement, widely understood as directed at the five Black and Latino teenagers arrested for the crime — all five of whom were exonerated in 2002 after another man confessed and DNA evidence confirmed it.
- **trumpbio**: The five defendants — later known as the Exonerated Five — served 6 to 13 years before DNA evidence and a confession from the actual perpetrator cleared them; New York City paid $41 million in a wrongful-conviction settlement. Trump has never apologized for the ad and, as recently as a 2024 presidential debate, falsely claimed the five had pled guilty — a claim that is not true and that the men are currently suing him over for defamation.
- **trumpbio**: Cemented Trump's public image as a dealmaker; Schwartz later became a public critic, stating he regretted helping build the persona.
- **trumpbio**: At a September 2024 presidential debate, Trump falsely claimed the five had "pled guilty" — no such plea exists; all five maintained innocence throughout trial. The Exonerated Five are suing him for defamation over the statement. [cite:aljazeera_cpf_lawsuit] As of this research, the case's resolution is not yet confirmed — flagged per this project's standing currency-discipline rule for ongoing litigation.
- **trumpbio**: The early 1990s brought the first wave of Trump-linked corporate bankruptcies (Taj Mahal, 1991; Trump Plaza and Trump Castle, both 1992) alongside the public collapse of his marriage to Ivana amid his relationship with Marla Maples, finalized in a 1992 divorce.
- **trumpbio**: The bankruptcy sequence is documented in full in the companion Trump Organization module; the divorce proceedings included Ivana's own account (later softened in a legal disclaimer) describing an incident she had once called rape in a deposition, which she later stated she did not intend in a literal or criminal sense.
- **trumpbio**: Taj Mahal (1991), Trump Plaza and Trump Castle (both 1992) — full documentation in the companion module.
- **trumpbio**: Trump married Marla Maples in 1993 (divorced 1999). He acquired the Miss Universe pageant organization in 1996. In 1999-2000, he briefly explored a Reform Party presidential bid, ultimately withdrawing.
- **trumpbio**: The marriage produced daughter Tiffany Trump, whose own independently-documented record is covered in the companion Tiffany Trump Architecture module.
- **trumpbio**: The Apprentice premiered in 2004, rebuilding Trump's public image around business-mogul competence for a mass television audience after the 1990s bankruptcies. He married Melania Knauss in 2005.
- **trumpbio**: The Apprentice's timing — arriving after, not before, the well-documented bankruptcy era covered in the companion Trump Organization module — is itself a notable sequencing fact: the TV persona was built in the aftermath of, not before, the business difficulties it helped the public forget.
- **trumpbio**: A ratings success that re-established Trump as a symbol of business success in popular culture, a decade after the documented 1990s casino bankruptcies.
- **trumpbio**: How they met, the competing documented accounts of the introduction, and her own record are covered in full in the companion Melania Trump Architecture module.
- **trumpbio**: Trump University launched in 2005, drawing fraud allegations that would eventually settle for $25 million. Trump Entertainment Resorts, the successor to his casino holdings, filed for bankruptcy again in 2009.
- **trumpbio**: Both threads — the Trump University fraud settlement and the casino-era bankruptcy sequence — are documented in full in the companion Trump Organization Architecture module, kept here as cross-references only.
- **trumpbio**: Trump became the most prominent promoter of the false "birther" claim that Barack Obama was not born in the US, sustaining the claim publicly for years before eventually acknowledging in 2016 that Obama was born in the US. On June 16, 2015, he announced his presidential campaign.
- **trumpbio**: The claim was false throughout, documented as such by Hawaii's own birth records at the time; Trump sustained it publicly for roughly five years before a brief, terse acknowledgment in September 2016 — a documented five-year gap between promotion and retraction worth stating plainly.
- **trumpbio**: From 1973 (the housing discrimination case) through the 2016 election, Trump and his businesses were named in a minimum of 3,500 legal actions, per USA Today's original analysis — with Wikipedia's own compiled figure now over 4,000 when related and follow-on cases are included. That's an average of over 116 filings per year for three decades.
- **trumpbio**: Close to half the cases involved gamblers who hadn't paid casino debts; the rest spanned real estate contract disputes, bankruptcy and loan fights, defamation suits, and over 100 separate business tax disputes. During just the campaign's first year (summer 2015-2016), Trump and his businesses averaged a new lawsuit filing every five days, split roughly 50/50 between suing and being sued.
- **trumpbio**: Sued the Chicago Tribune in 1984 over a report his planned hotel would be shorter than the Sears Tower; sued a labor union in 2011 for allegedly damaging his Las Vegas hotel's reputation; sued comedian Bill Maher for $5M after Maher jokingly offered that sum if Trump could prove he wasn't "the son of an orangutan."
- **trumpbio**: A month before the 2016 election, the Access Hollywood tape surfaced, capturing Trump making lewd remarks about women; he won the presidency regardless. His first term included the Trump Tower meeting and Mueller investigation, a first impeachment over a Ukraine phone call, the COVID-19 pandemic, and a second impeachment following the January 6th Capitol riot — the only president in US history impeached twice.
- **trumpbio**: A 2005 recording of Trump making lewd remarks about women; widely predicted to end his campaign, it did not — he won the election the following month.
- **trumpbio**: During the first term, multiple federal agencies, the Secret Service, the RNC, and foreign governments made documented payments into Trump-owned properties — most prominently the Trump International Hotel in Washington, leased from the government's own General Services Administration.
- **trumpbio**: CREW's tally puts total Secret Service spending at Trump properties near $2 million across the term; the DC hotel alone charged the Secret Service over $200,000 in the first year; foreign governments spent a documented $3.8 million at that hotel; the RNC paid $3,000/month; Trump's own inaugural committee spent $1 million there (the subject of the DC lawsuit documented in the companion Ivanka module). Separately, House Oversight found Trump had concealed over $1.1 billion in outstanding debts on his original 2011 GSA lease application — a documented omission on the application that won him the lease in the first place.
- **trumpbio**: CREW's compiled tally of FOIA'd Secret Service records found nearly $2 million spent at Trump-owned properties over the term. [cite:crew_secretservice_2m] The DC hotel alone charged over $200,000 in the first year, including a single $30,000 two-day bill. [cite:nbc_hotel_secretservice_200k] Mar-a-Lago separately charged roughly $63,700 in one three-month window.
- **trumpbio**: Foreign governments spent a documented $3.8 million at the hotel over the term; the RNC paid $3,000/month; Trump's inaugural committee spent $1 million there — the same payment documented in the companion Ivanka Trump module's Inaugural Committee scene. [cite:newrepublic_hotel_shakedown]
- **trumpbio**: House Oversight found Trump's 2011 GSA lease application included a 2008 financial statement reporting over $1.1 billion in outstanding loans across Chicago, Las Vegas, New York, and San Francisco properties — but that by 2009-2010, those same loans had been omitted from the financial statements actually submitted, concealing key information from the government agency deciding whether to grant him the lease. [cite:oversight_gsa_concealed_debts] **Written status: a documented finding from a congressional committee's own report — not an independently adjudicated fraud finding, but a specific, sourced allegation about the application process itself, distinct from the payment figures above.**
- **trumpbio**: In July 2019, Trump sued the House Ways and Means Committee, NY's Attorney General, and NY's tax commissioner — filed "in his capacity as a private citizen" — to block a new NY state law that would let the committee obtain his state tax returns.
- **trumpbio**: Trump's own filing argued the law violated his First Amendment rights because it was enacted "to discriminate and retaliate" against him for his politics — a real, documented legal argument, distinct from whether it succeeded. Every elected president since Nixon had voluntarily released tax returns before Trump; he did not, citing an ongoing audit — a claim independent tax experts have stated does not itself legally bar voluntary release.
- **trumpbio**: Filed after NY passed a law (the TRUST Act) letting the Ways and Means chairman request Trump's state tax returns. Trump's lawyer, Jay Sekulow, called the effort "presidential harassment." [cite:lawfare_ny_tax_suit_2019] NY AG Letitia James stated: "President Trump has spent his career hiding behind lawsuits."
- **trumpbio**: This 2019 case is the earliest documented instance in this module of Trump personally suing a government oversight body seeking his own financial records — a pattern that recurs, at far larger scale, in the 2026 IRS lawsuit documented in Scene dt17b.
- **trumpbio**: Following his 2020 election loss and the January 6th Capitol riot (documented in the companion Kushner and Don Jr. modules), Trump faced four separate criminal indictments between 2023-2024: a NY hush-money case, a Georgia election-interference case, a federal Jan. 6-related case, and a federal classified-documents case.
- **trumpbio**: Writer E. Jean Carroll sued Trump twice: once in 2022 (under NY's Adult Survivors Act, over an alleged 1990s assault) and once over his 2019 denial statements. A May 2023 jury found Trump liable for sexual abuse (not rape, under NY's narrower legal definition) and defamation, awarding $5 million. A second jury in January 2024 awarded $83.3 million over the 2019 statements specifically.
- **trumpbio**: Both verdicts have been upheld on appeal by the 2nd Circuit — the panel specifically found the "degree of reprehensibility" of Trump's conduct "remarkably high, perhaps unprecedented," rejecting his presidential-immunity argument. As of this research (Sept. 2026), Trump has petitioned the Supreme Court to hear a further appeal of the $83.3M verdict specifically; the PBS NewsHour reported the payment obligation was temporarily paused pending that review. This is a real, still-unresolved appellate question — not a closed matter either way.
- **trumpbio**: A jury found Trump liable for sexually abusing Carroll in a department store dressing room in the 1990s (a claim a judge later stated a reasonable jury could describe as "rape" in common usage, though the specific NY legal statute's narrower definition wasn't met) and for defaming her in 2022 denial statements. Awarded $5M.
- **trumpbio**: A second jury, deliberating less than three hours, awarded Carroll $18.3M in compensatory damages and $65M in punitive damages specifically to deter continued defamation. [cite:gulfnews_carroll_verdict2] Trump maintained he had never met Carroll and that she fabricated the claim.
- **trumpbio**: The 2nd Circuit unanimously upheld both verdicts, rejecting Trump's presidential-immunity defense and declining a full-court rehearing. [cite:yahoo_carroll_appeal_fails] Trump petitioned the US Supreme Court in July 2026 specifically on the $83.3M verdict, arguing the lower courts "never even decided whether presidential immunity applies." [cite:scotusblog_carroll_cert] As of this research, the Supreme Court has not resolved this petition — genuinely unresolved, not a closed matter.
- **trumpbio**: On May 30, 2024, a Manhattan jury convicted Trump on all 34 felony counts of falsifying business records — the first time a former US president has been found guilty of a crime. Weeks later, on July 13, he survived a sniper's bullet at a Butler, PA rally that killed one attendee and wounded his ear; a second attempt followed September 15 at his Florida golf club.
- **trumpbio**: A Manhattan jury convicted Trump on all 34 felony counts of falsifying business records related to a hush-money payment to Stormy Daniels ahead of the 2016 election. [cite:cbc_hush_money_verdict] Each count carried a maximum four-year sentence.
- **trumpbio**: Thomas Crooks fired eight shots at a Butler campaign rally, wounding Trump's ear and killing one attendee before Secret Service snipers killed Crooks. [cite:wiki_butler_assassination] A House task force's Dec. 2024 final report examined the security failures involved.
- **trumpbio**: Ryan Routh concealed himself near the fence of Trump's golf course; a Secret Service agent spotted his rifle and opened fire before Routh could, and he was later captured. [cite:wiki_florida_assassination] Routh was convicted on all federal counts in Sept. 2025, including attempted assassination of a major presidential candidate.
- **trumpbio**: This ruling is the single most direct legal mechanism explaining why the federal Jan. 6 case never reached trial — even conduct a prosecutor might frame as unofficial became far harder to prove once evidence of official-acts context was ruled inadmissible, and the case was formally dropped months later following the 2024 election under separate DOJ policy. The ruling also directly reached into the NY state case: Trump's team cited it in a failed bid to overturn his conviction and used it, more successfully, to help secure the lightest possible sentence.
- **trumpbio**: Special Counsel Jack Smith filed a 165-page sealed brief in Sept. 2024 attempting to narrow the case to purely unofficial conduct under the new standard; the case was ultimately dropped following Trump's 2024 win, per longstanding DOJ policy against prosecuting a sitting president — a separate, policy-based reason layered on top of the immunity ruling's practical effect.
- **trumpbio**: Trump's team cited the ruling to argue the NY jury verdict must be set aside because prosecutors improperly introduced evidence of official acts — the trial judge rejected this and let the conviction stand. But the same immunity landscape shaped the sentencing outcome: on Jan. 10, 2025, Judge Merchan imposed an "unconditional discharge" — no prison, no fine, no probation, the most lenient sentence legally available — explicitly citing the unprecedented posture of sentencing a president-elect. [cite:wiki_ny_prosecution] [cite:scotusblog_ny_sentencing] The Supreme Court itself declined to block the sentencing, noting the "burden" of a brief virtual hearing ending in discharge was "relatively insubstantial." His appeal of the underlying conviction remains pending.
- **trumpbio**: No single cause explains why none of Trump's legal exposure resulted in incarceration or barred his return to office. At least five independent, documented mechanisms combined: a Supreme Court immunity ruling limiting what evidence federal prosecutors could use; DOJ's own longstanding policy against prosecuting a sitting president; a Supreme Court ruling that only Congress, not states or courts, can enforce the 14th Amendment's disqualification clause against a federal candidate; a lenient state sentencing outcome explicitly shaped by the unprecedented posture of sentencing a president-elect; and civil verdicts (Carroll, the fraud case) that, even at their largest, carry financial rather than custodial consequences and remain under appeal.
- **trumpbio**: Every mechanism documented here is real, specific, and legally distinct — this module states each precisely rather than collapsing them into either "he did nothing wrong" or "the system let him escape." The Colorado Supreme Court, notably, actually found on the merits that Trump "engaged in insurrection" — the US Supreme Court did not disturb that specific factual finding; it ruled on a separate, narrower question of who has power to act on it.
- **trumpbio**: The Colorado Supreme Court, after a trial, found Trump "engaged in insurrection" and ordered him off the primary ballot under the 14th Amendment's Disqualification Clause. [cite:wiki_trump_v_anderson] The US Supreme Court unanimously reversed — but on a narrower ground: "States have no power under the Constitution to enforce Section 3 with respect to federal offices, especially the President." [cite:scotus_anderson_opinion] Only Congress, by statute, can enforce this clause against a federal candidate — and Congress has passed no such enforcement statute since Reconstruction. **The Court did not rule that Trump didn't engage in insurrection — it ruled that Colorado had no authority to make that determination stick for a federal race.**
- **trumpbio**: Trump won the November 2024 presidential election, becoming only the second US president to serve non-consecutive terms. He was inaugurated for a second term on January 20, 2025.
- **trumpbio**: Trump and top officials were evacuated after an armed man opened fire in the lobby of the White House Correspondents' Dinner venue; a suspect was arrested and charges were pending as of this research. [cite:aljazeera_assassination_timeline] Also documented: a June 2026 report on Trump's active efforts to formally clear his impeachment and conviction record, per Forbes. [cite:forbes_clearing_record_2026]
- **trumpbio**: On January 29, 2026, sitting President Trump — joined by Don Jr., Eric Trump, and the Trump Organization — sued the IRS and Treasury Department for $10 billion over a 2019-2020 tax-return leak by IRS contractor Charles Littlejohn (already criminally convicted and serving five years). On May 18, 2026, the DOJ — which Trump's own administration controls — settled by creating a $1.776 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund." On July 13, 2026, a federal judge voided the entire settlement, calling it "collusion."
- **trumpbio**: The underlying leak and Littlejohn's conviction are real and undisputed. What a federal judge specifically found improper was the settlement's structure: US District Judge Kathleen Williams ruled the executive branch agencies had colluded "to manipulate the judicial process," characterizing the deal as designed to secure Trump and his family blanket immunity from past tax audits while creating a fund to compensate self-described "lawfare" victims — effectively Trump's own political allies, funded by the DOJ's judgment fund, a perpetual taxpayer appropriation.
- **trumpbio**: Filed in Miami federal court, alleging the IRS and Treasury failed to take "mandatory precautions" against contractor Charles Littlejohn's 2019-2020 leak of Trump's tax data to the NYT and ProPublica. [cite:nbc_irs_suit_filed] The suit calculated damages at $1,000 per individual who viewed the leaked information in news coverage — reaching the $10B figure. Littlejohn had already pleaded guilty and was sentenced to five years, separately.
- **trumpbio**: Trump's own DOJ agreed to fund a $1.776 billion settlement, structured as a new "Anti-Weaponization Fund" paid from the DOJ's judgment fund — a perpetual taxpayer appropriation. [cite:cnbc_settlement_fund] Congressional Democrats called it a "slush fund" for Trump political allies who'd faced prosecution under the prior administration. Trump's team stated any money he personally received would go to charity.
- **trumpbio**: Williams voided the settlement, finding the executive branch agencies (including Trump's own DOJ) had colluded "to manipulate the judicial process," and that the deal was structured to secure Trump and his family "immunity from past tax audits" while establishing the compensation fund. [cite:courthousenews_settlement_voided] 93 members of Congress had separately filed a brief the same week calling the suit an unconstitutional "collusive" action.
- **trumpbio**: Rather than litigate the voided settlement further, Trump's lawyers filed a "self-executing" notice of voluntary dismissal with prejudice — permanently ending the case the moment it was filed, before the court could rule on whether it even had jurisdiction to hear it, and two days ahead of a court deadline to address that exact question.
- **trumpbio**: This case is structurally unlike any other in this research program: the plaintiff (Trump personally) sued a defendant (the IRS/Treasury) that reports, ultimately, to him as president, and the settlement was negotiated and approved by his own Department of Justice. A federal judge found this specific structure improper — not the existence of a real underlying grievance (the Littlejohn leak, independently and criminally proven), but the mechanism used to resolve it. This is a documented structural finding, stated precisely rather than generalized into a claim about every lawsuit Trump has ever brought against government bodies.
- **trumpbio**: On the campaign trail, Trump and JD Vance promised to release the DOJ's Epstein files. In February 2025, newly confirmed AG Pam Bondi said a client list was "sitting on my desk right now to review" and that DOJ had a "truckload" of information. By July 2025, DOJ reversed course, stating no client list existed and no further files would be released — reversing five months of public promises.
- **trumpbio**: A documented private warning sits directly between the promise and the reversal: the Wall Street Journal and CNN both reported Bondi told Trump in a May 2025 meeting that his own name appeared in the files. CNN's own analysis piece is titled, in its own words, "Timeline suggests Trump team changed its tune... after Trump was told he was in them" — that is CNN's stated editorial analysis of the documented sequence, not an independently proven causal fact. This module states the sequence plainly and labels the causal claim as CNN's own framing, consistent with the discipline applied to every other contested causal question in this research program.
- **trumpbio**: Bondi told Fox News a client list was "sitting on my desk right now to review," calling it a Trump directive; DOJ released ~100 pages (flight logs, a redacted contact book, a masseuse list) on Feb. 27 to invited conservative influencers — material largely already previously known. [cite:npr_bondi_timeline] Bondi later said she'd been referring to case files generally, not a client list specifically.
- **trumpbio**: The Wall Street Journal reported, and CNN independently corroborated, that Bondi told Trump in a May 2025 meeting his own name appeared in the Epstein files. [cite:cnn_timeline_changed_tune] Separately, Sen. Durbin's July 2025 letter alleged FBI staff reviewing the documents had been instructed to specifically "flag" any mention of Trump — a claim DOJ documents later released this year indicate did occur, per American Oversight's tracking; Bondi declined under Senate questioning to say who issued that instruction. [cite:americanoversight_bondi_testimony]
- **trumpbio**: DOJ and FBI issued a joint memo stating there was no evidence of a client list, blackmail scheme, or foul play in Epstein's death, and that no further files would be released — reversing the prior five months of promised transparency. [cite:npr_bondi_timeline] Trump told reporters: "It's pretty boring stuff. It's sordid, but it's boring," and that no further credible information remained to release. [cite:nbc_trump_frustrated_bondi]
- **trumpbio**: Facing sustained bipartisan pressure, Congress passed and Trump signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act in November 2025, legally compelling further DOJ disclosure regardless of the administration's prior July reversal — leading to the large December 2025 document releases documented in the next scene.
- **trumpbio**: The eventual December 2025 release (11,000+ files, ~30,000 pages, forced by the Transparency Act) confirmed Trump's name appears in the files over 1,000 times — a mention count that, per this project's standing rule, is not itself evidence of anything. Specific, tiered findings within that volume: confirmed flight-log presence on Epstein's plane; a contested, actively-litigated birthday letter; and Ghislaine Maxwell's own on-record exculpatory statement.
- **trumpbio**: Real, documented, primary-sourced findings exist at multiple tiers here — genuinely more, and more specific, than what was found regarding Jared Kushner or Melania Trump in the companion modules. This module tiers them explicitly rather than collapsing them into one verdict, consistent with the claim-decomposition discipline used throughout this entire research program.
- **trumpbio**: Per a DOJ-released internal email discussing Epstein's flight records, Trump was listed as a passenger on at least 8 flights on Epstein's plane between 1993-1996, with Maxwell also present on at least 4. [cite:pbs_flight_logs_dec2025] On one 1993 flight, Epstein and Trump were the only two passengers listed. On another, the passengers were Epstein, Trump, and a redacted individual who was 20 at the time. Two further flights included two women, names redacted, identified in the same email as potential witnesses in Maxwell's criminal case. **Written status: documented flight-log presence, independently confirmed via a primary DOJ-released document — a real, specific, primary-source-confirmed fact. It documents travel together, not conduct.**
- **trumpbio**: … WSJ reported (July 2025) a "bawdy" letter bearing Trump's name in a 2003 leather-bound album Maxwell compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday — containing a hand-drawn outline of a woman and a typed message ending with a line about a "wonderful secret," signed "Donald." Trump called it fake and sued WSJ and Rupert Murdoch for defamation. In September 2025, the Epstein estate — under House Oversight subpoena — released a redacted version of the actual birthday album, which does include a drawing and greeting that appear to bear Trump's signature. [cite:britannica_epstein_timeline] **In April 2026, a federal judge dismissed Trump's defamation suit, finding he failed to show the "actual malice" standard required for a public figure's libel claim — a ruling about the legal standard for the lawsuit, not an independent authentication of the letter itself.** Trump has vowed to refile. Nearly 50 prominent individuals, including Bill Clinton, contributed to the same birthday album — a documented fact worth noting for scale and context.
- **trumpbio**: In DOJ-released audio and transcripts of Deputy AG Todd Blanche's August 2025 interview with Ghislaine Maxwell, Maxwell stated she never saw Trump "in any inappropriate setting." [cite:axios_files_released_list] This is a named, on-record statement from arguably the single most relevant possible witness, and is included here for balance, with the same weight given to any other named source in this research program.
- **trumpbio**: A Dec. 2025-released email states investigators found a photo of Trump and Maxwell together while forensically examining Steve Bannon's iPhone in June 2021. [cite:cbs_dec2025_release] No date, location, or context for the photo itself was documented in this research pass — a real, newly surfaced data point, with its significance genuinely undetermined absent further information. Separately, the FBI confirmed a different circulating item — an alleged Epstein-to-Larry-Nassar letter making a crude Trump reference — was forensically confirmed **fake**, a documented example of DOJ actively identifying fabricated material in the same release, not just material implicating anyone.
- **donjr**: Donald Trump Jr. is tracked in this module as his own subject, distinct from his father's and distinct from his siblings', per the family-conflation guardrail applied throughout this research program. He has been a Trump Organization executive, a co-investigated party in state and federal legal matters, a central figure in the 2016 Russia investigation, an author, and — currently — a venture capital partner whose fund has grown dramatically since his father's re-election.
- **donjr**: A Trump Organization executive whose June 2016 meeting with Russian nationals became a central focus of the Mueller investigation, who was a named Trump Foundation director in a settled self-dealing case, who remained a defendant in the NY civil fraud case after his sister was dismissed, and who — in a genuinely documented moment of daylight from the public narrative — privately urged his father to intervene as the Capitol was being stormed on Jan. 6.
- **donjr**: Born Dec. 31, 1977. Eldest child of Donald Trump and Ivana Trump. This module treats his business career, the 2016 Russia-meeting episode, his legal record, and his current ventures as separate documented threads.
- **donjr**: Donald Trump Jr. graduated from the University of Pennsylvania (Wharton School) with a degree in real estate and finance, then joined the Trump Organization, eventually becoming Executive Vice President of Development and Acquisitions — the same title Ivanka Trump held, reflecting the two siblings' parallel positions in the family company.
- **donjr**: Trump Jr. authored Triggered: How the Left Thrives on Hate and Wants to Silence Us (2019) and Liberal Privilege: Joe Biden and the Democrats' Defense of the Indefensible (2020), both commercially successful political books published during his father's presidency and re-election campaign.
- **donjr**: On June 9, 2016, Trump Jr. met at Trump Tower with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya, after being told via email that she would provide "official documents and information that would incriminate Hillary" as "part of Russia and its government's support for Mr. Trump." Jared Kushner and campaign chairman Paul Manafort also attended. Trump Jr. responded to the initial offer, "if it's what you say I love it."
- **donjr**: The Mueller Report found insufficient evidence to prosecute — not because the offer or the meeting's premise wasn't documented (it was, extensively, via emails Trump Jr. himself later released), but because prosecutors couldn't prove the participants knowingly violated the specific federal law barring campaigns from accepting foreign assistance. Both halves of this are true simultaneously and shouldn't be collapsed into either "nothing happened" or "proven collusion."
- **donjr**: British publicist Rob Goldstone emailed Trump Jr. on behalf of Russian pop star Emin Agalarov, offering documents that would "incriminate Hillary and her dealings with Russia" as part of "Russia and its government's support for Mr. Trump." [cite:factcheck_trumptower] Trump Jr. replied within minutes: "if it's what you say I love it especially later in the summer."
- **donjr**: Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya met with Trump Jr., Jared Kushner, and campaign chairman Paul Manafort at Trump Tower. Per testimony released by the Senate Judiciary Committee, participants largely agreed the promised "dirt" on Clinton did not materialize — Trump Jr. told congressional investigators he was "willing to listen" but had no way of assessing the information's source. [cite:cbs_trumptower_transcripts]
- **donjr**: Trump Jr. was investigated alongside his sister Ivanka by the Manhattan DA over allegedly inflated Trump SoHo sales claims — the case dropped after Trump's personal attorney secured a direct meeting with the DA, bypassing line prosecutors. Full documentation lives in the companion Kushner Architecture module.
- **donjr**: Investigated alongside Ivanka Trump; case dropped in 2012 following a donor-attorney's direct meeting with DA Cyrus Vance Jr. Full detail, including the specific email evidence and donation timeline, lives in the companion module.
- **donjr**: Trump Jr. was, alongside Ivanka and Eric, a named director of the Donald J. Trump Foundation, subject to the 2018 NY AG self-dealing lawsuit and the resulting dissolution and $2M settlement.
- **donjr**: In February 2018, Trump Jr. traveled to India to promote Trump-branded luxury real estate, sharing a platform with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at a business summit where he was originally scheduled to give a foreign-policy address on "Reshaping Indo-Pacific Ties." After Senate criticism, the talk was retitled a "fireside chat."
- **donjr**: Sen. Robert Menendez formally wrote to the US Ambassador to India specifically because Trump Jr. was sharing a summit stage with a head of government while promoting his father's brand — a real, documented, named ethics concern raised in writing at the time, not a retrospective criticism.
- **donjr**: Menendez wrote to the US Ambassador to India stating he was "concerned that Mr. Trump's speech will send the mistaken message that he is speaking on behalf of the President." [cite:deccan_india_trip] The scheduled foreign-policy address was retitled a "fireside chat" following the criticism. The White House stated the State Department would treat him "like any other American on private business."
- **donjr**: Trump Jr. was named in the 2022 NY AG civil fraud lawsuit alongside his father, brother Eric, and the Trump Organization. Unlike Ivanka, who was dismissed in 2023 on statute-of-limitations grounds specific to her departure timing, Trump Jr. remained a defendant through the trial, the 2024 judgment, and its 2025 reversal on appeal.
- **donjr**: The specific reason Ivanka was dismissed (her departure predated the tolling agreement) simply didn't apply to him — he remained active in the company throughout the relevant period. Full documentation of the case's complete arc, including the split appellate rationale, lives in the Trump Organization Architecture module.
- **donjr**: Trump Jr. spoke at the Jan. 6 rally preceding the Capitol riot. As the riot was underway, he privately texted White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows — alongside several Fox News hosts — urging his father to publicly condemn the violence immediately, stating "he's got to condemn this s— ASAP" and "we need an Oval Office address... it has gone too far and gotten out of hand."
- **donjr**: As the riot was underway, texted Chief of Staff Mark Meadows: "We need an Oval Office address. He has to lead now. It has gone too far and gotten out of hand," followed by "He's got to condemn this s— ASAP. The Capitol Police tweet is not enough." [cite:cnn_meadows_texts] Meadows replied, "I'm pushing it hard. I agree." The texts were revealed by the Jan. 6 committee via Rep. Liz Cheney in Dec. 2021, part of a larger batch that also included similar urgent messages from Fox News hosts Sean Hannity, Laura Ingraham, and Brian Kilmeade. [cite:nbc_meadows_texts] Trump Jr. declined to comment on the texts when asked by NBC News.
- **donjr**: Trump Jr. is a partner at 1789 Capital, a venture fund aligning investing with conservative political values. Before he joined and before his father's 2024 re-election, the fund managed roughly $150 million. By late 2025, per Reuters reporting, it had grown to over $1 billion — with a portfolio that has expanded into defense contractors, AI startups, and companies like SpaceX, xAI, and Neuralink that ethics experts say could benefit from federal contracts and regulatory changes the administration controls.
- **donjr**: A roughly 7x growth in assets under management, coinciding precisely with Trump Jr.'s joining the fund and his father's re-election, invested substantially in sectors (defense, AI, companies like SpaceX/xAI/Neuralink) directly subject to the administration's own regulatory and contracting decisions — a documented structural conflict, with the caveat that Reuters' own reporting states it could not determine whether any specific investment was made because of advance knowledge of policy decisions.
- **donjr**: A venture fund explicitly built to "align equity investing with conservative political values." Trump Jr. joined as a partner; assets under management multiplied roughly 7x following his joining and his father's 2024 re-election. [cite:msnbc_1789capital]
- **donjr**: Reuters reporting found the fund's holdings include defense contractors and AI startups that ethics experts say could benefit from federal contracts and deregulatory policy shifts the administration controls — and specifically noted that Trump administration policy changes have already benefited at least three 1789-backed companies. Reuters explicitly stated it could not determine whether any of 1789's investments were made with advance knowledge of coming policy decisions — a documented, appropriate limit on the finding, not resolved either way.
- **donjr**: Donald Trump Jr.'s documented record includes a genuine business career, a central role in the most scrutinized episode of the Russia investigation (with a documented no-charge outcome), shared legal exposure with his siblings in the Foundation and civil fraud cases, a real-time documented push for his father to act on Jan. 6, and a current venture fund whose growth trajectory is the clearest dollar-for-dollar conflict-of-interest pattern in this entire four-module research program.
- **donjr**: ESTABLISHED: the Trump Tower meeting's occurrence and the Mueller Report's no-charge finding (both true simultaneously); the India trip's documented ethics concern; the Meadows texts, including their content showing him pushing for intervention; 1789 Capital's growth trajectory. NOT ESTABLISHED: any claim that 1789 Capital's specific investment decisions were made with advance knowledge of policy — Reuters' own reporting explicitly stopped short of that finding, and so does this module.
- **erictrump**: Eric Trump is tracked in this module as his own subject, distinct from his father's and siblings'. He has been a Trump Organization executive since the mid-2000s, the founder of a children's cancer charity that became the subject of a major investigative finding, a named Foundation director, a defendant in the NY civil fraud case, and — currently — a co-founder of the family's crypto venture and the most publicly visible face of its Gulf real estate expansion.
- **erictrump**: Born Jan. 6, 1984. Third child of Donald Trump and Ivana Trump. This module treats his charity, his corporate role, his legal exposure, and his current ventures as separate documented threads.
- **erictrump**: Eric Trump graduated from Georgetown University with a degree in finance and management, then joined the Trump Organization, becoming Executive Vice President of Development and Acquisitions alongside his brother.
- **erictrump**: Rose to Executive Vice President alongside Donald Trump Jr., overseeing real estate development and acquisitions — now the most publicly visible face of the company's Gulf real estate and crypto expansion (see Scenes e06-e07).
- **erictrump**: Eric Trump founded a charity in 2006 that raised over $16.3 million for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital through an annual golf tournament at Trump National Golf Club, Westchester. A June 2017 Forbes investigation found the Trump Organization had charged the charity hundreds of thousands of dollars for use of facilities Eric Trump publicly and repeatedly claimed were donated for free — with more than $1.2 million in charity spending having no documented recipient beyond the Trump Organization itself.
- **erictrump**: IRS filings reviewed by Forbes show tournament costs rising from roughly $59,000 (2012) to $322,000 (2015) — proceeds from a children's cancer charity flowing to the family's own golf course, plus more than $500,000 re-donated to other charities "connected to Trump family members or interests," several of which then paid to hold their own events at Trump courses. Charity experts told Forbes the costs charged "defy any reasonable cost." A follow-up Forbes report in Jan. 2018 found Eric Trump continued telling the press the course was "100% free" a full year after the story broke, even as the charity's own new filing showed a $99,000 payment for goods and services the filing itself valued at $184,000.
- **erictrump**: Per IRS filings reviewed by Forbes, tournament costs charged by the Trump Organization to the charity rose sharply starting in 2011 — reportedly after Donald Trump personally discovered the club hadn't been billing his son's charity and ordered it to start. [cite:abc_eric_foundation] A 2014 filing also shows an $87,665 payment to a separate Trump golf course in Washington, DC, for a related fundraising event.
- **erictrump**: More than $500,000 was re-donated by the Eric Trump Foundation to other charities, several of which had documented connections to Trump family members or interests — at least four of which subsequently paid to hold their own golf tournaments at Trump courses, per Forbes. [cite:cnn_eric_foundation]
- **erictrump**: A January 2018 Forbes follow-up, based on a newly obtained filing, found Eric Trump had continued publicly claiming the golf course was "100% free" even after the original story — while the charity's own filing showed a $99,000 payment for services it valued at $184,000. Two former board members told Forbes they'd believed all funds went to the hospital. The charity, renamed Curetivity, had by then suspended operations following the 2016 election. [cite:forbes_followup_lied]
- **erictrump**: Distinct from his own St. Jude charity, Eric Trump was also a named director of the family's Donald J. Trump Foundation, subject to the 2018 NY AG self-dealing lawsuit.
- **erictrump**: A completed legal case with documented consequences, including a one-year bar from NY nonprofit leadership — kept as a cross-reference. Worth noting explicitly: Eric Trump has now been connected to two separate charity-related findings (his own foundation and the family Foundation) — kept as two independently-scored threads, not blended into one.
- **erictrump**: Eric Trump was named in the 2022 NY AG civil fraud lawsuit and, like Don Jr. and unlike Ivanka, remained a defendant through the trial, the 2024 judgment, and its 2025 reversal on appeal.
- **erictrump**: Full documentation of the case's complete arc, including the split appellate rationale, lives in the Trump Organization Architecture module — kept here as a cross-reference to avoid duplicating the same finding.
- **erictrump**: Eric Trump is a co-founder of World Liberty Financial, alongside Don Jr., Barron Trump, and Zach Witkoff — the family's crypto venture behind the USD1 stablecoin, which drew over $2 billion from Abu Dhabi state-linked entities.
- **erictrump**: Full documentation of WLF's UAE investment, the Justin Sun/SEC-case connection, and the OCC bank-charter approval lives in the Trump Organization Architecture module. Eric Trump is the co-founder most publicly associated with promoting the venture at industry events.
- **erictrump**: Co-founded alongside Don Jr., Barron Trump, and Zach Witkoff. Publicly represented the venture at crypto industry conferences, including alongside Justin Sun.
- **erictrump**: Eric Trump is the family member most publicly visible at the launches of the company's $10B+ in announced Gulf projects with Dar Global — Dubai, Jeddah, Riyadh, Oman, and the Qatar-adjacent Doha project.
- **erictrump**: Full documentation of the specific deals, dollar figures, and the foreign-government-deal line the company says it hasn't crossed lives in the Trump Organization Architecture module. Eric Trump's specific role — public-facing announcer and dealmaker — is the operational counterpart to Don Jr.'s role managing the trust that holds the underlying assets.
- **erictrump**: Eric Trump married Lara Trump (then Lara Yunaska) in 2014. Lara went on to co-chair the RNC and later host a Fox News show — documented in the companion Trump Organization Architecture module's extended family network scene.
- **erictrump**: Kept as a brief cross-reference — Lara Trump's own institutional roles (RNC co-chair, Fox News host) are her own documented record, tracked separately per the family-conflation guardrail, not treated as an extension of Eric Trump's own record.
- **erictrump**: RNC co-chair (2024), then Fox News host — her own independently-scored record, not inherited from or attributed to Eric Trump.
- **erictrump**: Eric Trump's documented record includes a genuine decades-long executive career, a children's cancer charity whose own IRS filings and Forbes' reporting document real, unresolved questions about where donor money went, shared legal exposure with his brother in the Foundation and civil fraud cases, and current leadership roles in the family's most active financial ventures.
- **erictrump**: ESTABLISHED: the Eric Trump Foundation's billing pattern and the 2018 follow-up showing continued misrepresentation, both sourced to IRS filings and Forbes' named reporting; his co-founder role at WLF; his public role in the Gulf deals. NOT ESTABLISHED: any criminal charge resulting from the NY AG's or Congress's stated concerns about the charity — both raised the issue formally; neither produced a charge in this research pass.
- **ivanka**: Ivanka Trump is tracked in this module as her own subject, with her own documented record — distinct from Donald Trump's and distinct from Jared Kushner's, per the family-conflation guardrail applied throughout this research program. She has been, at different points, a model, a television personality, a real estate executive, a fashion-brand founder, a White House senior official, and a private citizen again. Each role is treated as its own documented thread.
- **ivanka**: Born Ivana Marie Trump, Oct. 30, 1981, in Manhattan — the second child of Donald Trump and Ivana Trump. This module treats her business career, her marriage, and her government role as three separate documented threads, never blended into a single narrative.
- **ivanka**: Frederick Trump (Ivanka's great-grandfather) emigrated from Germany and built a fortune in Klondike-era hospitality before returning to the US. His son Fred Trump built a large NYC outer-borough real estate empire; Donald Trump inherited and expanded that business. A 1918-award-winning New York Times investigation (Pulitzer Prize, Explanatory Reporting, 2019) documented that Fred Trump transferred well over $400 million to his children — including Donald — through mechanisms the investigation characterized as including outright tax fraud, sharply reducing the tax owed on that transfer.
- **ivanka**: An immigrant-family real estate business, real and substantial — but the wealth transfer from Fred Trump to his children was the subject of a Pulitzer Prize-winning NYT investigation documenting specific tax-avoidance and undervaluation schemes, a finding about the family's wealth origin that predates Ivanka's own career and financial position by decades.
- **ivanka**: A 2018 New York Times investigation (which won the 2019 Pulitzer Prize for Explanatory Reporting) documented that Fred Trump transferred more than $400 million to his children over decades, using mechanisms the investigation described as including instances of outright tax fraud and significant undervaluation of assets to reduce the tax owed. This is widely reported, award-recognized journalism, not a single-source claim — flagged here at a general level consistent with this document's practice of not reproducing extensive verbatim reporting detail.
- **ivanka**: Donald Trump's own business and legal record is a subject of its own scale and is not comprehensively covered in this Ivanka-focused module — referenced here only as the origin point connecting Fred Trump's wealth transfer to Ivanka's own eventual position in the family business and her personal financial disclosures (Scene 9).
- **ivanka**: Ivanka Trump attended Choate Rosemary Hall, a prominent boarding school, before earning a B.S./B.A. in economics from the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School (after briefly attending Georgetown), graduating cum laude. As a teenager, she modeled for major fashion houses including Tommy Hilfiger and Versace — a short-lived career that nonetheless gave her early exposure to branding and public image.
- **ivanka**: After a stint at Forest City Enterprises, Ivanka joined the Trump Organization as an executive, eventually becoming Executive Vice President of Development and Acquisitions. From 2006 to 2015, she appeared as a judge/advisor on her father's reality show The Apprentice — a documented, decade-long public role that predates any government position.
- **ivanka**: A real, substantial corporate role (Trump Organization EVP) ran in parallel with nearly a decade on a reality television show co-starring her father — both are documented facts, kept separate from any claim about her later government qualifications.
- **ivanka**: Worked on the company's real estate and hotel management initiatives. Reportedly earned roughly $35M in salary from the Trump Organization over her career, per aggregated reporting on the family's finances.
- **ivanka**: G-III Apparel Group, which manufactured Ivanka Trump-branded clothing alongside Calvin Klein and DKNY, disclosed in an SEC filing that wholesale revenue for the line rose 61% to $47.3M for the fiscal year ending Jan. 31, 2017 — barely 2% of G-III's $2.39B total net sales. Her own July 2017 ethics disclosure valued the entire brand trust at "more than $50 million." Both figures are far below the "$800 million" figure she has publicly cited.
- **ivanka**: Ivanka Trump was a named director of the Donald J. Trump Foundation. In 2018, New York's Attorney General sued the Foundation and its directors — Trump, Ivanka, Donald Jr., and Eric — alleging over a decade of illegal self-dealing and unlawful political coordination with the 2016 campaign. The Foundation dissolved as part of a court-supervised settlement; Trump personally admitted to misusing Foundation funds and was ordered to pay $2 million in damages.
- **ivanka**: A real, completed legal case: the NY AG's suit alleged the Foundation "functioned as little more than a checkbook" for Trump's business and political interests; the settlement required dissolution, a personal admission from Trump of misusing funds, a $2M damages payment, and mandatory ethics training for all three named children as a condition of the settlement — a documented legal consequence, not merely an allegation.
- **ivanka**: NY AG Barbara Underwood's office, following a 21-month investigation, sued in June 2018 alleging "a shocking pattern of illegality," including unlawful 2016 campaign coordination and repeated self-dealing to benefit Trump's personal and business interests. [cite:npr_trumpfoundation_sued]
