- **natoarch**: At the 2014 Wales Summit, NATO members agreed to move toward spending at least 2% of GDP on defense within a decade. This followed Russia's annexation of Crimea and reflected concern that European members were underinvesting in defense while relying on US capabilities. Historically, only a handful of members met the 2% threshold — the US, UK, Greece, and Estonia were consistent above-2% spenders through much of the 2010s. The Russia-Ukraine war (2022) accelerated European defense spending. By 2024, NATO reported 23 of 32 members meeting or exceeding 2%. The US spends approximately 3.4% of GDP on defense (2024) — well above the threshold. The 2% pledge has been a documented source of tension, particularly under Trump who argued allies were 'free-riding' on US defense provision. [cite:nato_defense_spending_2024]
- **healtharch**: (1) Why U.S. drug prices are structurally higher than every comparable country — the documented baseline that predates both Trump terms and both parties' recent promises; (2) the PBM architecture — the documented middleman layer that intercepts drug rebates before they reach consumers; (3) what was promised this cycle and what was actually delivered, including the 'Great Healthcare Plan' and MFN deals; (4) the coverage side — the largest documented healthcare policy change of the second term: 11.8-16 million people losing Medicaid, scored on its own terms.
- **healtharch**: Trump's April 2025 executive order directed a review of PBM 'middlemen' roles and a more transparent pharmaceutical value chain [cite:kff_pbm]. The administration also proposed a rule requiring greater PBM compensation transparency in employer health plans [cite:kff_pbm]. The IRA (2022) required PBMs to pass through 100% of rebates to employer plans in Medicare Part D. The 'Great Healthcare Plan' (January 2026) stated it would 'end the kickbacks' paid by PBMs [cite:thehill_ghp] — but as of this build, no legislation eliminating PBMs or mandating full rebate passthrough has passed, and the FTC's stronger proposed remedies (divestiture of vertically integrated pharmacy operations) have not been implemented.
- **healtharch**: The administration's May 2018 'American Patients First' blueprint promised to slash drug prices through drug importation, rebate reform, international price referencing, and ending 'gag clauses' preventing pharmacists from telling patients about cheaper options. Most provisions requiring legislative or broad administrative action were not delivered by the end of the first term — an independent academic analysis concluded 'the Trump administration has not yet been able to fulfill the major campaign promises, primarily the ones requiring legislative and/or administrative action' [cite:bhfs_promises]. The one Most Favored Nation rule attempted was blocked in court before taking effect.
- **healtharch**: The 'Great Healthcare Plan,' released January 15, 2026, proposed redirecting ACA subsidies from insurers to patients, PBM reform, transparency requirements, and drug-pricing commitments [cite:whitehouse_ghp]. NBC News noted it was released 'the same day Affordable Care Act open enrollment ends in most states' and 'offered few details and largely restated proposals Trump has previously outlined' [cite:nbc_ghp]. It requires Congress to act — the same Congress that, as of this build, has not passed any standalone drug-pricing legislation in this term.
- **healtharch**: A complete accounting of every major first-term drug-pricing claim and its documented outcome, including the mechanisms that were proposed with fanfare and then quietly dropped, and the insulin $35 cap that is frequently attributed to Trump but was codified into law by a subsequent administration.
- **healtharch**: Trump's May 2018 'American Patients First' blueprint was a 44-page plan covering rebate reform, biosimilar competition, drug importation, price transparency, and international reference pricing [cite:bhfs_t1]. HHS Secretary Azar acknowledged at the unveiling: 'It's going to be months for the kind of actions that we need to take... it took decades to erect this very complex interwoven system.' Financial analysts noted the proposals were 'somewhat gentler than many feared' — pharma and PBM stocks rallied the same day the plan was announced.
- **healtharch**: The first-term administration publicized voluntary commitments from insulin manufacturers to lower list prices and created a Part D Senior Savings Model capping insulin co-pays at $35/month for participating plans — a real, documented step. However: the Part D model was voluntary (not all plans participated); it was later incorporated into and strengthened by the Biden administration's IRA, which mandated the $35 cap for all Medicare Part D beneficiaries; and Trump's own April 2025 executive order reviving an insulin pricing mechanism was a re-issue of a 2020 order whose rules were delayed, never took effect, and were rescinded by Biden in 2021 [cite:legalclarity_insulin]. The $35 Medicare cap Americans see today is IRA law, not the executive order.
- **healtharch**: A peer-reviewed academic analysis of Trump's first-term drug-pricing record concluded: 'the Trump administration has not yet been able to fulfill the major campaign promises, primarily the ones requiring legislative and/or administrative action' [cite:tandfonline_t1]. The actions that were completed — the gag-clause ban, accelerated generic approvals, hospital price transparency requirements — were real but incremental. The structurally significant moves (rebate rule, mandatory importation, MFN pricing) were either withdrawn, blocked in court, or never implemented [cite:bhfs_t1].
- **healtharch**: This closing scene documents the cross-term pattern visible across both Trump administrations' drug-pricing records — not as an assertion about intent, but as a documented sequence of outcomes that can be checked claim by claim against the evidence already built into this module.
- **healtharch**: Eight years of drug-pricing promises across two Trump terms. The 2.78x structural gap: unchanged. The PBM architecture: intact. The mechanisms that would have changed the structure (rebate rule, mandatory MFN): withdrawn or blocked. The mechanisms that survived: voluntary, incremental, or codified by another administration. The 3.1% BLS drop of 2026: real, primarily attributed to an earlier administration's IRA negotiation by independent experts. The 'highest to lowest' framing: not supported by any independent global benchmark. The documented beneficiaries: consistently the companies between drugs and patients.

Extrapolated across 10 trips at an average midpoint of $3-4M per trip in aircraft costs alone: $30-40M in Air Force One costs for overseas travel in term 1. Add DoD equipment airlift (comparable cost) and Secret Service advance teams: the overseas travel total alone likely reaches $80-120M for term 1 — making it the single largest category of presidential travel cost, larger than domestic golf travel.

- **vanityprojects**: The Secret Service Director told USA Today in August 2017 that the agency was protecting 42 people under Trump — up from 31 under Obama — because Trump's adult children and their spouses required protection when conducting Trump Organization business overseas [cite:citizen_family][cite:georgetown_ethics]. This represented a 35% increase in the protected population, with a corresponding increase in personnel, travel costs, and coordination overhead.
- **vanityprojects**: Melania Trump's decision to remain in Trump Tower in Manhattan rather than move to the White House immediately (she stayed through June 2017 while Barron finished the school year) cost New York City approximately $500,000 per day in Police Department overtime and security logistics to secure the building [cite:fortune_pace]. New York City officials requested federal reimbursement; the federal government's contribution to these costs was disputed. Trump Tower requires securing 58 floors of a mixed-use skyscraper in one of the world's busiest pedestrian areas — structurally more expensive than the already-secured White House or Camp David.
- **vanityprojects**: By August 2017 — seven months into Trump's first term — approximately 1,100 Secret Service employees were working overtime hours in excess of federal pay caps [cite:citizen_family]. The director stated plainly: the issue was 'not one that can be attributed to the current Administration's protection requirements alone, but rather has been an ongoing issue for nearly a decade due to an overall increase in operational tempo' — but the 35% increase in protectees under Trump accelerated the problem significantly. The Secret Service requested an additional $60 million for its FY2018 budget; the Office of Management and Budget initially rejected that request [cite:georgetown_ethics].
- **vanityprojects**: Public Citizen documented multiple overseas business trips by Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. that required Secret Service protection — including a Uruguay trip and multiple India trips connected to Trump Organization real estate projects [cite:citizen_family]. The Secret Service agents who accompanied them stayed in the same luxury hotels where Trump-branded events were held, with hotel costs paid by the government. Public Citizen's analysis noted that these trips generated both security costs (taxpayer) and real estate marketing value (Trump Organization) simultaneously — the same structural self-dealing dynamic documented in the golf travel scene.
- **vanityprojects**: In June 2017, Representatives Tom O'Halleran and Ruben Gallego introduced an amendment to the annual defense authorization bill requiring the Air Force to submit regular reports to Congress documenting all presidential travel costs — specifically including costs for trips to Trump-owned or operated properties [cite:fox4_pentagon]. The amendment was considered during the House Armed Services Committee's markup of the $696 billion defense bill. Republicans on the committee blocked it. The Air Force Secretary had confirmed to O'Halleran in a letter that Air Force costs for Trump's first 120 days totaled $15.8 million — but declined to provide a breakdown. Without the amendment, those reports were never required.
- **vanityprojects**: Throughout both terms, the White House declined to release: total presidential travel costs per trip; total presidential travel costs per year; a breakdown of costs by agency (Air Force, Secret Service, DoD, Coast Guard); and the aide accommodation records that would quantify how much flowed back to Trump properties. The White House's consistent position: these are classified or security-sensitive. This refusal is documented — it is why Judicial Watch spent years filing FOIA requests and obtained only the Air Force component [cite:judicial_foia][cite:judicial_year1].
- **vanityprojects**: The Georgetown Business Ethics Assessment Professor Peter Jaworski of Georgetown University told reporters in 2017: 'Every president has to go on vacation, everybody needs a bit of time off. - **homelandsecfull**: Trump's Jan. 25, 2017 executive order dramatically broadened interior-enforcement priorities and directed DHS to expand 287(g). Participating agencies grew from 32 (end of Obama) to 152, with expiration-date guardrails removed. In 2018, the administration's "zero tolerance" border policy resulted in the systematic separation of migrant families.
- **homelandsecfull**: A principled rollback of aggressive Trump-era enforcement tactics.
- **homelandsecfull**: The documented record shows neither the full rollback his campaign implied nor continuity with the prior administration — a genuine middle position: freezing growth while declining to unwind what already existed, a choice his own transition materials' stated goals (voiding all Trump-era 287(g) agreements) did not fully match in practice.
- **homelandsecfull**: Biden's own campaign Agenda for the Latino Community included voiding all Trump-era 287(g) agreements — but as of the end of his term, the administration had taken no action to actually do so, despite ACLU and partner-organization pressure to remove agencies with documented profiling records. [cite:aic_biden_tracker]
- **homelandsecfull**: On Trump's first day back in office, a new executive order called for dramatic 287(g) expansion, explicitly reviving the task-force model Obama had terminated in 2012. Agreements grew 600% in the first eight months. Separately, the administration has quietly expanded family separation by connecting child-welfare data (from the Office of Refugee Resettlement) with ICE enforcement, leading to over 12,000 arrests per internal data reviewed by Reuters.
- **homelandsecfull**: The number of local agencies opting into 287(g) grew 600% in the second Trump term's first eight months — reviving the task-force model specifically terminated in 2012 following DOJ profiling investigations. [cite:aclu_287g_expansion]
- **homelandsecfull**: Per an independent tracking report, Palantir has received over $1.8 billion in federal funding since the second Trump term began, including a new $1 billion purchase agreement. [cite:truthout_surveillance_report]
- **homelandsecfull**: DHS spent over $220 million on an ad campaign warning unauthorized immigrants to leave the country, heavily featuring Secretary Noem — including a widely covered ad of her on horseback at Mount Rushmore. Invoices show a single subcontractor was paid $286,137, including a $20,000 horse-rental fee and nearly $4,000 for hair and makeup. Asked directly who approved the spending, Noem said Trump did; Trump denied it; she was removed from the role within weeks.
- **homelandsecfull**: The dollar figures come from actual invoices obtained by senators and shared with CNN — not estimates or characterizations, but documented line items ($20,000 horse rental, $3,800 hair/makeup, a $60,000 signing bonus, $100,000+ in labor costs). The direct Trump-Noem contradiction over approval, followed by her removal within the same news cycle, is itself a documented sequence of events.
- **homelandsecfull**: Under Senate questioning, Noem said Trump personally approved the spending. Trump denied doing so. Shortly after, Trump announced Noem would leave DHS by the end of the month, replaced by Sen. Markwayne Mullin — a documented, direct factual contradiction between the president and his own Cabinet secretary, resolved by her removal rather than a public reconciliation of the conflicting accounts.
- **homelandsecfull**: Like nearly every Cabinet secretary position, there is no statutory requirement that a DHS Secretary have any specific law-enforcement, national-security, or homeland-security experience. The position requires only presidential nomination and Senate confirmation by majority vote — the same structural gap already documented in the companion Trump Organization module regarding presidential candidacy itself.
- **homelandsecfull**: Like most Cabinet secretary positions, DHS Secretary requires only presidential nomination and Senate confirmation — no codified law-enforcement, national-security, or homeland-security experience requirement exists in statute. This mirrors the structural finding already documented in the companion Trump Organization Architecture module regarding presidential-candidate qualifications generally: the constitutional/statutory design simply does not include a substantive experience bar for this kind of position.

- **fdaarch**: The pharmaceutical industry is the most powerful lobbying force in Washington, spending more on federal lobbying than any other industry sector in most years. In 2022, the pharmaceutical and health products industry spent over $370 million in federal lobbying. Former FDA Commissioner Scott Gottlieb became a Pfizer board member 3 months after leaving FDA — and had sat on GSK's board before being named FDA Commissioner by President Trump. Nearly 340 former congressional staffers work for pharmaceutical companies or their lobbying firms. The result is an agency whose legislative environment — the laws it must enforce, the authorities it holds, the funding it receives — is substantially shaped by the industry it regulates.

- **tariff**: This module treats tariffs as a policy instrument with a 130-year documented track record, not a Trump-specific story. It walks through: how tariffs have actually been used before (and what happened each time); exactly how the money moves; what was promised this cycle; what the documented record shows; who benefits; and what history and this cycle together teach.
- **tariff**: McKinley (1890), Smoot-Hawley (1930), the Reagan/Bush steel and motorcycle tariffs (1983-2003), and both the 2018-2020 and 2025-2026 Trump tariff regimes — including the 2026 Supreme Court ruling and what replaced it. This module cross-references, rather than duplicates, the fuller policy-by-policy scorecards already built in this series' first- and second-term modules.
- **tariff**: Before checking the record, the specific claims worth checking, stated in Trump's own words where available, across both tariff cycles.
- **tariff**: Across both the 2018-2020 and 2025-2026 tariff cycles, Trump made a consistent set of specific, checkable claims: foreign countries pay the tariffs, not Americans; tariffs would revive domestic manufacturing broadly; tariffs would shrink the trade deficit; tariffs would not cause inflation; and tariffs could eventually replace the federal income tax entirely.
- **tariff**: Trump repeatedly stated there was 'no inflation' from his tariffs even as they took effect, a claim made as recently as mid-2025 [cite:lieu_cpi] — a specific, dated, checkable statement rather than a general policy position.
- **tariff**: Most strikingly, Trump stated at a December 2025 Cabinet meeting: "I believe that at some point in the not-too-distant future, you won't even have income tax to pay because the money we're taking in is so great" [cite:cbsnews_replacetax]. He repeated a version of this at the 2026 State of the Union, saying tariffs would 'substantially replace the modern-day system of income tax' [cite:yahoo_27times]. This claim gets its own dedicated scene later in this module (a06), because the arithmetic is unusually clean to check.
- **tariff**: In 2002, steel-consuming industries employed 12.8 million against 170,000 steelworkers — 57 to 1 [cite:cato_60years]. Trump's own 2018 steel/aluminum tariffs produced a similar ratio: economists calculated roughly 12,700 protected jobs at a documented cost of about $815,000 in broader economic drag per job (per this series' first-term module). The consistent documented pattern: tariffs create concentrated, visible winners in one industry while spreading costs thinly across many other industries and consumers who are individually less organized to lobby against it.
- **tariff**: The Hill's analysis found fully replacing income tax revenue would require an approximate 80% tariff on all imports — more than triple the rates actually imposed — and that's before accounting for the fact that trade volume itself shrinks as tariff rates rise (substitution, rerouting, retaliation), a dynamic economists call the tariff Laffer curve [cite:yahoo_taxplan2025]. Two economists cited in that analysis estimated the realistic maximum revenue obtainable from tariffs, under the most tariff-friendly assumptions, at about $500 billion a year — Trump's actual tariffs, as imposed, raise less than a third of even that theoretical ceiling [cite:yahoo_taxplan2025].
- **tariff**: Trump's 2025 tariff regime rested on a novel legal claim: that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 — a law previously used for sanctions against foreign adversaries — authorized the President to impose broad-based tariffs on all trading partners via declared emergency, without any Act of Congress [cite:bracewell_scotus2]. Every court that reviewed this claim, at every level, found it wrong.
- **tariff**: Smoot-Hawley: 25 nations retaliated [cite:utah_smoot]. Bush 2002: WTO ruled the tariffs illegal, triggering EU retaliation threat [cite:salon_bush2002]. Trump 2018-2019: China retaliated, costing US agricultural exporters billions and requiring a federal farm-aid bailout. Trump 2025: China retaliated; exemption carve-outs were negotiated. Retaliation is not a partisan interpretation of tariff history — it is what trading partners have documented as doing every time the U.S. has raised tariffs sharply since 1930.
- **gasarch**: The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco found that presidential party affiliation explains less than 10% of the variation in gas prices over time. The price of gasoline is set primarily by global crude oil markets (50-60% of retail price), controlled by OPEC+ — a legal sovereign cartel the US president cannot legally compel. The EIA documented that US crude oil production reached an all-time high under Biden in 2023 — and prices were still high, because OPEC cut production to offset US output. Trump's claim that he would lower gas prices to $2 by 'unleashing' US production is contradicted by basic economics: the US already produces more oil than it can use domestically. Additional US production is offset by OPEC cuts. The 'Drill Baby Drill' policy does not lower retail gas prices.
- **gasarch**: … The president of the United States has four documented levers affecting retail gasoline prices: (1) Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases — temporary, typically moving prices 5-20 cents for weeks; (2) Regulatory policy on drilling permits — affects US production with a 1-3 year lag and is offset by OPEC production adjustments; (3) Sanctions on oil-producing nations — Iran, Russia, Venezuela — which reduce global supply and raise prices; (4) Dollar policy, indirectly, through the Federal Reserve, which the president does not control. None of these levers can produce the $2 gas prices Trump promised or the instant price drops he claimed. The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco's research found presidential party explains less than 10% of gas price variation.

When politicians — Trump being the most documented example — use gas prices as an economic scorecard, they are using a metric that economists explicitly exclude from economic health measurements. The political appeal: gas prices are visible, daily, and emotionally resonant.
- **gasarch**: OPEC+ is a cartel of 22 sovereign nations coordinating oil production to maintain prices above a target floor. It controls approximately 50% of global oil supply and over 70% of the world's proved reserves. When US production increases under any president, OPEC offsets it with production cuts — a documented pattern across multiple administrations. Biden increased US production to record highs in 2023. OPEC cut 1.66 million barrels per day in April 2023. Prices remained high. Trump's 'Drill Baby Drill' promise faces the same arithmetic: additional US barrels are offset by OPEC reductions. The cartel manages the price floor. The US president manages less than it. This is not analysis — it is the documented operational history of how oil markets respond to US production changes.

Individual tax provisions were made temporary, set to expire at the end of 2025. - **work**: The Fair Labor Standards Act (1938) guarantees time-and-a-half overtime past 40 hours a week — for non-exempt employees. But the FLSA's 'white-collar exemption' lets an employer classify any executive, administrative, or professional employee earning above a federal salary floor as exempt from that guarantee entirely. In 2024, the Department of Labor tried to raise that floor substantially. A federal court vacated the rule nationwide in November 2024, and the Trump administration abandoned the appeal in 2025 — meaning the threshold reverted to, and currently sits at, $684 a week: $35,568 a year.

- **t1**: Gross federal debt rose from about $19.95 trillion (Jan 2017) to about $27.75 trillion (Jan 2021) — an increase of roughly $7.8 trillion, about 40% [cite:debt_treasury]. CRFB had calculated in 2016, before the term began, that eliminating the debt in eight years would require cutting roughly two-thirds of federal spending or sustaining ~16% real annual growth versus a ~2.1% baseline — and separately projected Trump's proposed policy mix would nearly double the debt within a decade, a projection that proved close to the actual trajectory [cite:debt_crfb].
- **t1**: In a March 2016 Washington Post interview, Trump said he could 'get rid of' the then-$19 trillion debt over eight years; in April 2016 he told Fortune he'd 'rather not be so aggressive' without giving a revised figure [cite:debt_reason].
- **t1**: Common Core was a set of state-adopted (not federally mandated) K-12 academic standards. Trump repeatedly promised to eliminate it and 'bring education locally' — a promise that ran into the basic fact that the federal government never controlled it in the first place.
- **t1**: PolitiFact's Trump-O-Meter closed the term at 25 promises kept, 23 compromised, and 54 broken across 102 total tracked pledges [cite:politifact_final]. This scene and the next log the major foreign-policy, judicial, and remaining domestic promises in brief — grouped by theme rather than given individual scorecards, since most don't carry a real 'helped rich vs. helped middle/working class' axis.
- **t1**: PolitiFact's final Trump-O-Meter report closed the term with 25 promises rated Kept, 23 rated Compromise, and 54 rated Broken out of 102 tracked pledges [cite:politifact_final] — the complete reference count this module's 13 major-policy scorecards and these two grouped scenes are drawn from and checked against.
- **t2**: This module covers President Trump's second term, January 20, 2025 through the present build date of September 1, 2026 — roughly 20 months into a 48-month term. Nine major policies get full scorecard treatment; the rest are logged in two reference scenes. Every claim tied to an active court case or unresolved legislative fight is tagged with its status as of this build.
- **t2**: Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R.1) on July 4, 2025 — the central piece of his second-term domestic agenda, making the 2017 tax cuts permanent, adding new tax exemptions on tips and overtime, boosting border-security funding, and cutting Medicaid/SNAP spending [cite:aaf_hr1].
- **t2**: … Opportunity Zones were made a permanent feature of the tax code ('OZ 2.0'), continuing a program Brookings found sent 75% of its money to real estate rather than job-creating business investment in its first cycle [cite:brookings_oz2]. And despite repeated promises across both of Trump's terms to close it, the carried-interest loophole benefiting private-equity and hedge-fund managers was left completely unchanged: 'the OBBBA does not include any change to the tax treatment of carried interests' [cite:skadden_obbba].
- **t2**: On April 2, 2025, Trump used IEEPA to impose a global tariff regime far broader than the first term's. Courts unanimously found this exceeded presidential authority at every level, culminating in a February 2026 Supreme Court ruling; the administration has since had to refund tens of billions in collected tariff revenue.
- **t2**: Trump used the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) — a 1977 sanctions law never before used this way — to impose a 10% global baseline tariff plus country-specific 'reciprocal' rates on nearly every U.S. trading partner, framed as ending decades of unfair trade [cite:steptoe_scotus].
- **t2**: On taking office, Trump signed executive orders declaring an 'invasion' at the southern border and deploying military personnel, framing a goal of one million deportations per year and the largest deportation operation in U.S. history.
- **t2**: Trump established the Department of Government Efficiency on his first day in office, appointing Elon Musk to lead it with a mandate to cut waste, fraud, and abuse — the goal was publicly stated as up to $2 trillion in annual federal savings.
- **t2**: The 43-day shutdown, Oct 1 - Nov 12, 2025, surpassed the previous record (35 days, 2018-2019, also under Trump) [cite:capitolwatch_shutdown]. It began over a fight tied directly to this module's ACA scorecard: Democrats sought to extend expiring ACA premium tax credits as a condition of funding; the standoff went unresolved for 43 days.
- **t2**: The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on June 30, 2026 that the order violates the 14th Amendment as interpreted since 1898 — a final, unappealable defeat [cite:naacpldf_birthright]. On August 6, 2026, Trump signed a new order attempting a narrower version of the same goal [cite:asianlaw_birthright] — a documented fact worth noting on its own, independent of how that new order eventually fares in court.
- **t2**: Trump signed Executive Order 14160 on his first day in office, attempting to deny automatic citizenship to children born in the U.S. to parents who are undocumented or on temporary status — directly contradicting the Supreme Court's 1898 ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark on the 14th Amendment [cite:naacpldf_birthright].
- **t2**: On August 6, 2026 — more than a month after losing 6-3 at the Supreme Court — Trump signed a new executive order again attempting to deny birthright citizenship to certain groups, based on parental origin and actions [cite:asianlaw_birthright]. This is a documented fact, not an inference: the timeline (loss June 30, new order Aug 6) is itself the finding.
- **t2**: Trump made versions of this claim repeatedly, including at the State of the Union: that Most Favored Nation deals took the U.S. from the highest global drug prices to the lowest [cite:citizen_soutu]. The claim is unqualified — it does not specify which drugs, which patients, or which payment method it applies to.
- **t2**: On Inauguration Day 2025, Trump again withdrew the U.S. from the Paris Agreement, declared a national energy emergency, and paused new wind-power leasing — reversing the prior administration's re-entry into Paris and its wind-energy support.
- **t2**: On January 20, 2025 — his first day back in office — Trump signed Executive Order 14162 beginning a second U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement, declared a 'national energy emergency,' and paused new wind-power leasing on federal lands [cite:congress_paris2][cite:opb_paris2].
- **t2**: World Liberty Financial, a crypto venture founded by Trump and his family in 2024, has taken in hundreds of millions from foreign state-linked investors and received a first-of-its-kind bank charter from a regulator the president appointed — while the president's administration simultaneously sets the regulatory rules for the entire crypto industry.
- **t2**: World Liberty Financial (WLFI) was founded in 2024 by Trump, his family, and outside partners, selling a token with 'little practical function beyond signaling support for the company,' per contemporaneous analysis. His administration simultaneously sets cryptocurrency regulatory policy.
- **t2**: Four days before Trump's inauguration, lieutenants of Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan — the UAE's national security adviser, brother of its president — signed a contract putting $500 million into WLFI in exchange for 49% equity [cite:fortune_wlfi_sheikh]. Separately, Abu Dhabi state fund MGX invested $2 billion more in May 2025, tying the deal to using the Trump family's USD1 stablecoin for transactions with Binance [cite:wiki_wlfi]. The administration then approved AI chip exports to the UAE that a prior administration had restricted over concerns the chips could reach China [cite:wiki_wlfi] — the sequence, not an allegation about intent, is the documented finding here.
- **t2**: A Trump-appointed national bank regulator (the OCC) granted a WLFI subsidiary, World Liberty Trust Co., conditional approval for a bank charter — the first time in U.S. history a company owned by a sitting president's family has received one [cite:abc_wlfi_bank]. Separately, KuCoin — a crypto exchange that partnered with WLFI in 2025 — received a favorable CFTC settlement in March 2026 on a case originally brought under the prior administration [cite:wiki_wlfi]. A White House spokesperson stated the president's assets are in a trust managed by his children and that there are 'no conflicts of interest' [cite:abc_wlfi_bank].
- **t2**: By December 2025, the Trump family had realized roughly $1 billion in proceeds from WLFI token sales, while still holding about $3 billion in unsold tokens [cite:wiki_wlfi] — the family reportedly receives 75% of net proceeds when WLFI sells tokens, plus a share of stablecoin profits. A House Judiciary Committee Democrats' report, citing Reuters reporting, put family crypto earnings at $800 million for just the first half of 2025 alone [cite:houseJud_wlfi] — attributed specifically to that report, since it comes from one party's committee staff rather than an independent audit. An NYT investigation separately found WLFI offered outside crypto startups 'guaranteed access' to executives in exchange for buying $10-30 million of its own coins, with one rejected pitch's target calling it 'a black spot on our industry' [cite:benzinga_wlfi].
